subject: ela
reviewStatus: ai-drafted: none of these items or passages has been human-reviewed; do not ship to students yet

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: Which sentence from the passage best supports the idea that Walt values the ferry’s place in people’s lives more than its practical use?
choices: “A man in a gray suit had even shaken Walt’s hand and said, ‘End of an era.’”
“Mostly it carries them across their own ordinary days.”
“Nell found a wooden crate beneath the pilot’s bench.”
“A bridge will be quicker.”
items.answer: “Mostly it carries them across their own ordinary days.”
items.explanation: Walt says the ferry carries people through their “ordinary days,” which shows he values its role in their lives, not just its use as transportation.

commonErrors.answer: “A bridge will be quicker.”
commonErrors.why: Picks a true statement that is about speed, not about what the ferry means to people.

commonErrors.answer: “Nell found a wooden crate beneath the pilot’s bench.”
commonErrors.why: Chooses a plot detail that sets up the discovery but shows nothing about Walt’s values.

commonErrors.answer: “A man in a gray suit had even shaken Walt’s hand and said, ‘End of an era.’”
commonErrors.why: Confuses another character’s respect for the ferry with Walt’s own view.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: Which statement best expresses a theme of the passage?
choices: Young people should help older relatives finish their life’s work.
Progress always replaces the old ways, so people should accept change quickly and stop dwelling on the past.
Old boats are more dependable than modern bridges are.
Everyday routines gain meaning from the human moments they hold, and those moments deserve attention.
items.answer: Everyday routines gain meaning from the human moments they hold, and those moments deserve attention.
items.explanation: Walt’s comments about “ordinary days” and people who “pause,” along with Nell’s display of the plates, develop the idea that everyday moments matter.

commonErrors.answer: Progress always replaces the old ways, so people should accept change quickly and stop dwelling on the past.
commonErrors.why: Over-generalizes; Walt accepts the bridge but the story is about noticing, not hurrying.

commonErrors.answer: Young people should help older relatives finish their life’s work.
commonErrors.why: Too narrow; focuses on Nell’s help rather than the idea the story develops.

commonErrors.answer: Old boats are more dependable than modern bridges are.
commonErrors.why: Reverses the story, where Walt admits the bridge will be quicker.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: How does Nell’s discovery of the crate of brass plates affect the story?
choices: She decides that the opening of the bridge should be delayed.
She becomes angry that her grandfather kept such a large secret hidden from her for so many years.
She comes to understand what the ferry means to her grandfather and decides to honor it.
She learns that the ferry earned more money than she believed.
items.answer: She comes to understand what the ferry means to her grandfather and decides to honor it.
items.explanation: After the plates and Walt’s explanation, Nell’s “chest shifted,” and the next morning she mounts the plates, showing a change in understanding.

commonErrors.answer: She becomes angry that her grandfather kept such a large secret hidden from her for so many years.
commonErrors.why: Assumes the discovery causes conflict; Nell never shows anger.

commonErrors.answer: She decides that the opening of the bridge should be delayed.
commonErrors.why: Confuses honoring the ferry with stopping the bridge; she never tries to stop it.

commonErrors.answer: She learns that the ferry earned more money than she believed.
commonErrors.why: Focuses on the cash box mentioned nearby, not the meaning of the plates.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: In the first paragraph, what does the phrase “a sort of museum piece” suggest about the ferry?
choices: It is valuable enough that collectors from across the region would want to buy it.
It is crowded each day with visitors who come to tour it.
It is fragile and must be handled with great care.
It is treated as a relic of the past rather than something people still need.
items.answer: It is treated as a relic of the past rather than something people still need.
items.explanation: The phrase, followed by “still happened to float,” suggests the ferry is now seen as an old object kept around mostly for the past.

commonErrors.answer: It is fragile and must be handled with great care.
commonErrors.why: Takes “museum” literally as a place for delicate objects.

commonErrors.answer: It is valuable enough that collectors from across the region would want to buy it.
commonErrors.why: Reads “museum piece” as high monetary value.

commonErrors.answer: It is crowded each day with visitors who come to tour it.
commonErrors.why: Assumes the ferry has become a tourist attraction, which the passage never says.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: Early in the passage Walt says, “They just wanted us,” and the narrator states that Nell “did not see the difference.” What effect does this create for readers?
choices: Readers begin to distrust Walt’s account of what the ferry means.
Readers sense Walt’s hidden point before Nell does, which builds anticipation for her change.
Readers are left unsure whether the ferry will really stop running.
Readers find humor in how foolishly Nell is behaving toward her grandfather throughout the scene.
items.answer: Readers sense Walt’s hidden point before Nell does, which builds anticipation for her change.
items.explanation: The narrator tells readers that Nell misses the difference Walt describes, so readers see his point early and wait for her to catch up.

commonErrors.answer: Readers begin to distrust Walt’s account of what the ferry means.
commonErrors.why: Reverses the effect; the narrator invites trust in Walt’s wisdom.

commonErrors.answer: Readers find humor in how foolishly Nell is behaving toward her grandfather throughout the scene.
commonErrors.why: Mistakes a gentle misunderstanding for a comic mistake; the tone is thoughtful.

commonErrors.answer: Readers are left unsure whether the ferry will really stop running.
commonErrors.why: Confuses the main conflict; the bridge’s opening is stated as certain.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: Which detail from the passage best supports the inference that Dev’s actions caused the crack in the bowl?
choices: He set the bowl beside the heater so it would be ready by Friday.
The wheel hummed like an old refrigerator.
The judge was a potter with clay ground into her knuckles.
He had already thrown forty bowls before this one and felt sure of himself.
items.answer: He set the bowl beside the heater so it would be ready by Friday.
items.explanation: Priya warns that clay “dries from the outside in,” and Dev still dries the bowl by the heater, which connects his rushing to the crack.

commonErrors.answer: He had already thrown forty bowls before this one and felt sure of himself.
commonErrors.why: True and shows confidence, but it does not explain how the crack formed.

commonErrors.answer: The wheel hummed like an old refrigerator.
commonErrors.why: A descriptive detail unrelated to the cause of the crack.

commonErrors.answer: The judge was a potter with clay ground into her knuckles.
commonErrors.why: Uses a detail about the judge, who only examines the result.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: How does the judge’s speech about the crack affect Dev’s decision at the end?
choices: It leads him to ask for the extra help he had earlier refused.
It convinces him that the judge was wrong to praise the glaze.
It causes him to argue with Priya about her warning.
It persuades him to enter a different contest.
items.answer: It leads him to ask for the extra help he had earlier refused.
items.explanation: After hearing that a flawed bowl teaches something, Dev walks to Ms. Carver’s desk and asks whether her offer still stands.

commonErrors.answer: It persuades him to enter a different contest.
commonErrors.why: Invents an outcome; the passage shows no new contest.

commonErrors.answer: It causes him to argue with Priya about her warning.
commonErrors.why: Reverses the ending, where Priya grins and supports him.

commonErrors.answer: It convinces him that the judge was wrong to praise the glaze.
commonErrors.why: Misreads the judge’s praise as an insult.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: The passage opens at the judging table and then moves back three weeks. How does this structure contribute to the story?
choices: It shows the result first, so readers wonder how the crack happened and read on for the cause.
It shows that the story is mostly about Priya’s memories.
It hides Dev’s mistakes until the very end of the story so that the final scene feels like a surprise.
It slows the plot so that the judge seems less important.
items.answer: It shows the result first, so readers wonder how the crack happened and read on for the cause.
items.explanation: Beginning with the crack creates curiosity, and the flashback then answers how it happened before returning to the judging.

commonErrors.answer: It hides Dev’s mistakes until the very end of the story so that the final scene feels like a surprise.
commonErrors.why: Dev’s mistakes appear in the flashback, well before the ending.

commonErrors.answer: It shows that the story is mostly about Priya’s memories.
commonErrors.why: Priya appears, but the point of view stays with Dev.

commonErrors.answer: It slows the plot so that the judge seems less important.
commonErrors.why: The judge’s scene is the story’s turning point, not minimized by the flashback.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: Which statement best expresses a theme of this story about Dev?
choices: Friends should avoid pointing out one another’s mistakes.
Talent is enough for success when a person practices carefully and works alone.
Judges should reward effort even when a piece is flawed.
Owning a mistake and learning from it matters more than the failure itself.
items.answer: Owning a mistake and learning from it matters more than the failure itself.
items.explanation: The judge says the difference is “whether it teaches them anything,” and Dev responds by asking for help, developing the theme of learning from error.

commonErrors.answer: Talent is enough for success when a person practices carefully and works alone.
commonErrors.why: Contradicts the story, where Dev’s confidence leads to failure.

commonErrors.answer: Friends should avoid pointing out one another’s mistakes.
commonErrors.why: Reverses Priya’s role; her warning was correct.

commonErrors.answer: Judges should reward effort even when a piece is flawed.
commonErrors.why: Shifts to a rule for judges; the story is about Dev’s growth.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: The narrator says Dev “waited for the verdict the way one waits for a wave.” What does this simile suggest?
choices: He felt calm and relaxed, as if at a beach.
He felt excited and hoped the judge would react in a dramatic way.
He felt tense and unable to stop what was about to happen.
He felt confused about what the judge meant to say.
items.answer: He felt tense and unable to stop what was about to happen.
items.explanation: A wave cannot be stopped, so the comparison, paired with his “stomach folded in on itself,” shows dread and helplessness.

commonErrors.answer: He felt calm and relaxed, as if at a beach.
commonErrors.why: Takes the water image literally and ignores his stomach “folding in.”

commonErrors.answer: He felt excited and hoped the judge would react in a dramatic way.
commonErrors.why: Confuses anticipation with eager hope; Dev is dreading the verdict.

commonErrors.answer: He felt confused about what the judge meant to say.
commonErrors.why: The judge has not yet spoken, so Dev cannot be confused by her words.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: Which detail the narrator observes in the garden best shows that her suspicion of Mr. Lindqvist was mistaken?
choices: He kneels beside the sunflowers at sunrise.
He notices her hiding behind the compost bin.
He is already in the garden when she arrives, long before the sun has fully risen.
He picks weeds and fruit already ruined by squirrels, not healthy tomatoes.
items.answer: He picks weeds and fruit already ruined by squirrels, not healthy tomatoes.
items.explanation: Picking weeds and spoiled fruit shows he is cleaning the garden, not stealing from it.

commonErrors.answer: He is already in the garden when she arrives, long before the sun has fully risen.
commonErrors.why: Fits her suspicion as much as it fits his innocence.

commonErrors.answer: He notices her hiding behind the compost bin.
commonErrors.why: Shows he is observant but not what he is doing in the garden.

commonErrors.answer: He kneels beside the sunflowers at sunrise.
commonErrors.why: Describes where he is without showing what he is doing.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: Which idea is most strongly developed by the narrator’s experience in the garden?
choices: Judging people by partial evidence can lead to unfair conclusions.
Quiet people are usually hiding something.
Neighbors should spend more time working in the garden.
Keeping detailed records is the best way to learn the truth about other people.
items.answer: Judging people by partial evidence can lead to unfair conclusions.
items.explanation: The narrator’s notes make Mr. Lindqvist look guilty, but his explanation reveals he was helping, so the story shows how partial evidence misleads.

commonErrors.answer: Quiet people are usually hiding something.
commonErrors.why: Reverses the story, in which the quiet man is shown to be kind.

commonErrors.answer: Keeping detailed records is the best way to learn the truth about other people.
commonErrors.why: The notebook leads the narrator astray, so it is not the lesson.

commonErrors.answer: Neighbors should spend more time working in the garden.
commonErrors.why: A detail of the setting, not the idea the plot develops.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: What does Mr. Lindqvist’s explanation in the garden reveal about his character?
choices: He is shy and responsible, and he keeps a promise to help a neighbor.
He is confused about how the community garden is run.
He is angry about being watched and wants to scare the narrator into leaving.
He is boastful and wants credit for caring for the garden.
items.answer: He is shy and responsible, and he keeps a promise to help a neighbor.
items.explanation: He says he promised to water Mrs. Alvarez’s plot and admits to being shy, which shows both his responsibility and his reason for not waving.

commonErrors.answer: He is angry about being watched and wants to scare the narrator into leaving.
commonErrors.why: His tone is polite and even encouraging.

commonErrors.answer: He is boastful and wants credit for caring for the garden.
commonErrors.why: He never seeks praise and shares the story only when questioned.

commonErrors.answer: He is confused about how the community garden is run.
commonErrors.why: He knows which plot belongs to whom and why it needs water.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: The narrator thinks Mr. Lindqvist is the thief, but readers can see signs that he is helping. What effect does this difference create?
choices: It makes readers feel sorry for the raccoons in the garden.
It builds suspense about whether Mr. Lindqvist is really guilty of stealing the tomatoes all summer.
It creates gentle humor, since readers recognize the narrator’s mistake before she does.
It makes readers distrust the narrator’s honesty in general.
items.answer: It creates gentle humor, since readers recognize the narrator’s mistake before she does.
items.explanation: Her detail-by-detail suspicion, such as the watering can and bulging pockets, is funny because readers can read those clues as signs of care.

commonErrors.answer: It builds suspense about whether Mr. Lindqvist is really guilty of stealing the tomatoes all summer.
commonErrors.why: The clues point away from guilt, so suspense is limited.

commonErrors.answer: It makes readers distrust the narrator’s honesty in general.
commonErrors.why: She is mistaken, not dishonest.

commonErrors.answer: It makes readers feel sorry for the raccoons in the garden.
commonErrors.why: The raccoons appear only in the last line.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: The passage opens with the narrator’s notebook entries and ends with “Entry seven stayed unwritten for a very long time.” How does this structure add to the story’s meaning?
choices: The blank entry shows that she has given up being a detective.
The entries show Zoe is the main detective in the story.
The entries prove that her suspicions about Mr. Lindqvist were correct from the very beginning.
The early entries show her suspicion, and the blank entry shows that her view has changed.
items.answer: The early entries show her suspicion, and the blank entry shows that her view has changed.
items.explanation: The numbered entries set up her theory, and the long pause over entry seven shows she no longer trusts that theory.

commonErrors.answer: The entries prove that her suspicions about Mr. Lindqvist were correct from the very beginning.
commonErrors.why: Reverses the plot, since the entries rest on misread clues.

commonErrors.answer: The blank entry shows that she has given up being a detective.
commonErrors.why: She still jokes about “another case file,” so she has not quit.

commonErrors.answer: The entries show Zoe is the main detective in the story.
commonErrors.why: Zoe is only a minor character who questions the case.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: Which lines from the poem best support the idea that the house holds a record of the speaker’s growth?
choices: “worn smooth by years of hurrying hands”
“The pale squares where the photographs once hung / look startled to be shown so plain”
“each small notch a year I stood against the wood / and stretched my spine”
“the boxes lean together / like tired gulls”
items.answer: “each small notch a year I stood against the wood / and stretched my spine”
items.explanation: The pencil notches on the doorframe mark each year the speaker grew taller.

commonErrors.answer: “the boxes lean together / like tired gulls”
commonErrors.why: Describes the packing, not the speaker’s growth.

commonErrors.answer: “The pale squares where the photographs once hung / look startled to be shown so plain”
commonErrors.why: Shows what is missing from the walls rather than growth over time.

commonErrors.answer: “worn smooth by years of hurrying hands”
commonErrors.why: Refers to many people’s use of the banister, not the speaker’s growth.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: Which statement best expresses a theme of the poem?
choices: Growing up means learning to argue with those in charge.
A house keeps its memories only while its photographs stay on the walls.
Leaving a place is hard, but the meaning of lived experience goes with us.
Moving is easier when a family labels and packs its belongings carefully ahead of time.
items.answer: Leaving a place is hard, but the meaning of lived experience goes with us.
items.explanation: The speaker says “leaving is a kind of carrying” and will keep the “height of every year,” so memories travel with the person.

commonErrors.answer: Moving is easier when a family labels and packs its belongings carefully ahead of time.
commonErrors.why: Picks up on the boxes and labels but ignores the poem’s deeper reflection.

commonErrors.answer: A house keeps its memories only while its photographs stay on the walls.
commonErrors.why: Reverses the ending, in which memories remain after the photographs are gone.

commonErrors.answer: Growing up means learning to argue with those in charge.
commonErrors.why: Over-reads the line about arguing with the ceiling, which is about growing taller.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: In the fourth stanza, the speaker runs a palm along the banister. What does this action lead to?
choices: It makes the speaker regret the decision to move away from the old house.
It prompts the speaker to realize that memories can be carried away.
It makes the speaker decide to ask the family to stay.
It reminds the speaker of an argument with a parent.
items.answer: It prompts the speaker to realize that memories can be carried away.
items.explanation: Right after touching the banister, the speaker says, “understand that leaving is a kind of carrying,” which marks the poem’s insight.

commonErrors.answer: It makes the speaker regret the decision to move away from the old house.
commonErrors.why: The speaker feels loss but never expresses regret.

commonErrors.answer: It makes the speaker decide to ask the family to stay.
commonErrors.why: No such decision appears; the speaker accepts the move.

commonErrors.answer: It reminds the speaker of an argument with a parent.
commonErrors.why: The only parent mentioned is remembered with fondness.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: In the third stanza, the pale squares on the wall “look startled to be shown so plain.” What is the effect of this wording?
choices: It gives the wall human feelings, making the empty house seem exposed.
It suggests the speaker was frightened by something unseen inside the house.
It shows the speaker is angry at the people who bought the house.
It suggests the walls were damaged during the move.
items.answer: It gives the wall human feelings, making the empty house seem exposed.
items.explanation: Calling the squares “startled” is personification that stresses how bare the rooms look.

commonErrors.answer: It suggests the speaker was frightened by something unseen inside the house.
commonErrors.why: Confuses the walls’ “startled” look with the speaker’s own fear.

commonErrors.answer: It suggests the walls were damaged during the move.
commonErrors.why: Reads “startled” as physical harm rather than personification.

commonErrors.answer: It shows the speaker is angry at the people who bought the house.
commonErrors.why: Nothing in the stanza mentions the buyers.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: In the last line, the speaker moves from the physical rooms to “some quiet room of me.” How does this shift develop the poem’s meaning?
choices: It contrasts a loud house with a quieter new home.
It shows that the speaker will return to the house soon.
It moves from outer objects to inner memory, showing the home lives on inside the speaker.
It repeats the first stanza’s picture to show that nothing about the house or the speaker has changed.
items.answer: It moves from outer objects to inner memory, showing the home lives on inside the speaker.
items.explanation: The final image turns the house into something internal, supporting the idea that memories continue after leaving.

commonErrors.answer: It repeats the first stanza’s picture to show that nothing about the house or the speaker has changed.
commonErrors.why: The first stanza’s ocean-in-a-shell image is transformed, not repeated.

commonErrors.answer: It shows that the speaker will return to the house soon.
commonErrors.why: The door “clicks shut” and no return is suggested.

commonErrors.answer: It contrasts a loud house with a quieter new home.
commonErrors.why: The new home is never described.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: Which sentence from the passage best supports the claim that the dance tells bees how valuable a food source is?
choices: Bees repeat the dance more often and with more energy when food is especially rich.
Because the sun moves across the sky, the dancers gradually change their angle over the day.
The straight, shaking stretch is the part that carries the message.
A quick, short waggle points to a patch just outside the hive.
items.answer: Bees repeat the dance more often and with more energy when food is especially rich.
items.explanation: Paragraph 4 links more repetitions and more energy to richer food, so the dance signals quality.

commonErrors.answer: The straight, shaking stretch is the part that carries the message.
commonErrors.why: Describes the part of the dance that matters, not food quality.

commonErrors.answer: A quick, short waggle points to a patch just outside the hive.
commonErrors.why: Shows distance, not value.

commonErrors.answer: Because the sun moves across the sky, the dancers gradually change their angle over the day.
commonErrors.why: Explains direction, not how rich the food is.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: Which statement best summarizes the central idea of the passage?
choices: Honeybees dance mainly to keep the hive warm and to keep the crowded colony together at night.
Honeybees use a patterned dance to share the direction, distance, and quality of food.
Honeybees depend on the sun more than other insects do.
Scientists have only recently learned how bees find flowers.
items.answer: Honeybees use a patterned dance to share the direction, distance, and quality of food.
items.explanation: Each body paragraph explains what the dance communicates: direction, distance, and how worthwhile a food source is.

commonErrors.answer: Honeybees depend on the sun more than other insects do.
commonErrors.why: Compares bees to other insects, which the passage never does.

commonErrors.answer: Scientists have only recently learned how bees find flowers.
commonErrors.why: The passage gives no timeline for the discovery.

commonErrors.answer: Honeybees dance mainly to keep the hive warm and to keep the crowded colony together at night.
commonErrors.why: Invents a purpose; the dance’s purpose is communication.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: According to the third paragraph, how are the dance’s angle and the sun connected?
choices: Gravity pulls the bees toward the sun, so they waggle upward.
The bees dance in direct sunlight on the hive’s outer wall to show other bees exactly where they should fly next.
The angle from straight up on the comb matches the angle from the sun’s direction to the flowers.
The sun’s brightness tells the bees how far away the flowers are.
items.answer: The angle from straight up on the comb matches the angle from the sun’s direction to the flowers.
items.explanation: The paragraph says straight up stands for the sun’s direction, so angles from vertical match angles from the sun.

commonErrors.answer: The bees dance in direct sunlight on the hive’s outer wall to show other bees exactly where they should fly next.
commonErrors.why: The dance happens inside the dark hive.

commonErrors.answer: Gravity pulls the bees toward the sun, so they waggle upward.
commonErrors.why: Mixes up gravity’s role as a vertical reference with the sun’s direction.

commonErrors.answer: The sun’s brightness tells the bees how far away the flowers are.
commonErrors.why: Confuses direction, shown by angle, with distance, shown by waggle length.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: In the third paragraph, “stand-in” is used in the phrase “straight up as a stand-in for the position of the sun.” What does “stand-in” mean here?
choices: a measuring tool that bees use to track the sun’s movement
a signal that warns of danger near the flowers
a barrier that blocks sunlight from the hive
a substitute that takes the place of something else
items.answer: a substitute that takes the place of something else
items.explanation: Straight up replaces the sun’s direction inside the hive, so “stand-in” means a substitute.

commonErrors.answer: a measuring tool that bees use to track the sun’s movement
commonErrors.why: Mistakes the phrase for a scientific tool.

commonErrors.answer: a barrier that blocks sunlight from the hive
commonErrors.why: Takes “stand” literally and thinks of something that blocks.

commonErrors.answer: a signal that warns of danger near the flowers
commonErrors.why: Associates the dance with warnings rather than directions.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: How does the second paragraph contribute to the development of the passage?
choices: It argues that the waggle dance is the most advanced insect behavior.
It describes the pattern of the dance so that later paragraphs can explain what each part means.
It lists the discoveries that scientists have made about bees over many years of careful study.
It compares the dance to the way humans use language.
items.answer: It describes the pattern of the dance so that later paragraphs can explain what each part means.
items.explanation: Paragraph 2 describes the straight run and loops, and paragraphs 3 and 4 then explain what the angle and length of the run mean.

commonErrors.answer: It argues that the waggle dance is the most advanced insect behavior.
commonErrors.why: Offers an opinion the passage never makes.

commonErrors.answer: It compares the dance to the way humans use language.
commonErrors.why: The comparison appears only in the final paragraph, and only in a general way.

commonErrors.answer: It lists the discoveries that scientists have made about bees over many years of careful study.
commonErrors.why: The paragraph describes movement, not discoveries.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: Which detail best supports the claim that measuring depth with a weighted rope was impractical in deep water?
choices: Sailors tied a lead weight to the end of a long rope.
The method worked well enough in harbors, according to the crews who used it every day.
The crew counted how much line ran out before the weight stopped.
The rope could drift or run out of length, and one measurement could take hours.
items.answer: The rope could drift or run out of length, and one measurement could take hours.
items.explanation: The second paragraph names drifting, running out of rope, and time as the problems in deep water.

commonErrors.answer: Sailors tied a lead weight to the end of a long rope.
commonErrors.why: Describes the method rather than its limits.

commonErrors.answer: The method worked well enough in harbors, according to the crews who used it every day.
commonErrors.why: True, but it describes where the method worked.

commonErrors.answer: The crew counted how much line ran out before the weight stopped.
commonErrors.why: Explains how the method was used, not why it failed.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: Which statement best summarizes the passage?
choices: Maps of the seafloor are mainly used to help ships avoid hazards.
Sailors long believed the seafloor was flat until multibeam sonar.
Ocean-floor mapping has moved from slow rope soundings to sound-based tools, though much remains unmapped.
Echo sounders have replaced every other way of studying the oceans, and ships now use them to map every part of the seafloor.
items.answer: Ocean-floor mapping has moved from slow rope soundings to sound-based tools, though much remains unmapped.
items.explanation: The passage traces rope soundings, echo sounders, and multibeam systems, and ends by noting how much is still unmapped.

commonErrors.answer: Echo sounders have replaced every other way of studying the oceans, and ships now use them to map every part of the seafloor.
commonErrors.why: Over-generalizes; the passage discusses depth mapping only.

commonErrors.answer: Maps of the seafloor are mainly used to help ships avoid hazards.
commonErrors.why: Too narrow; the passage names several uses.

commonErrors.answer: Sailors long believed the seafloor was flat until multibeam sonar.
commonErrors.why: Unsupported claim that is not in the text.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: How does the echo-sounder method compare with the rope-and-weight method?
choices: Both require the ship to stop moving during each measurement, but the echo sounder is much cheaper to run.
Both find the distance to the bottom, but the echo sounder uses the time an echo takes to return.
The rope method measures depth directly while the echo sounder measures only width.
Both depend on the speed of sound in water, but the rope method is less exact.
items.answer: Both find the distance to the bottom, but the echo sounder uses the time an echo takes to return.
items.explanation: Paragraphs 2 and 3 show both methods find depth, one using a lowered weight and the other timing an echo.

commonErrors.answer: Both depend on the speed of sound in water, but the rope method is less exact.
commonErrors.why: Gives the rope method a sound-based mechanism it does not have.

commonErrors.answer: The rope method measures depth directly while the echo sounder measures only width.
commonErrors.why: Mistakes what the echo sounder measures; it also measures depth.

commonErrors.answer: Both require the ship to stop moving during each measurement, but the echo sounder is much cheaper to run.
commonErrors.why: Cost and stopping are not discussed in the passage.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: In the first paragraph, the ocean floor is described as “as hidden as the far side of the moon.” What does this comparison suggest?
choices: The seafloor was long unseen and unknown to people.
The seafloor looks much like the surface of the moon.
The seafloor is uninteresting to scientists.
The seafloor is dangerous to approach.
items.answer: The seafloor was long unseen and unknown to people.
items.explanation: The far side of the moon cannot be seen from Earth, and the next sentence says the seafloor was “largely guesswork.”

commonErrors.answer: The seafloor is dangerous to approach.
commonErrors.why: Confuses hidden with dangerous.

commonErrors.answer: The seafloor looks much like the surface of the moon.
commonErrors.why: Reads the comparison as similarity of appearance.

commonErrors.answer: The seafloor is uninteresting to scientists.
commonErrors.why: Reads “hidden” as boring; the passage describes mapping as valuable.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: In the last paragraph, how does the author respond to the view that satellites have already mapped the seafloor?
choices: The author argues that satellites are too expensive to use.
The author dismisses the view without giving any reason.
The author agrees that satellites have replaced ships entirely and that sonar is now outdated for mapping.
The author grants that satellites show broad shapes but explains that sonar gives sharper detail.
items.answer: The author grants that satellites show broad shapes but explains that sonar gives sharper detail.
items.explanation: The author acknowledges satellites “suggest broad shapes” and then explains that sonar offers “far sharper detail.”

commonErrors.answer: The author dismisses the view without giving any reason.
commonErrors.why: Gives a reason; the paragraph explains satellites’ limits.

commonErrors.answer: The author agrees that satellites have replaced ships entirely and that sonar is now outdated for mapping.
commonErrors.why: Reverses the author’s response.

commonErrors.answer: The author argues that satellites are too expensive to use.
commonErrors.why: Cost is never mentioned in the paragraph.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: Which detail best supports the claim that green roofs can lower a building’s energy use?
choices: The extra layers insulate, so less energy is needed for heating and cooling.
Designers often choose sedum, a hardy plant that tolerates drought, wind, and poor soil.
Installation costs more than a conventional roof.
A green roof soaks up much of the rain that falls on it.
items.answer: The extra layers insulate, so less energy is needed for heating and cooling.
items.explanation: Paragraph 4 says the added layers insulate the building, reducing heating and cooling needs.

commonErrors.answer: Designers often choose sedum, a hardy plant that tolerates drought, wind, and poor soil.
commonErrors.why: Describes plant choice, not energy use.

commonErrors.answer: A green roof soaks up much of the rain that falls on it.
commonErrors.why: Supports the water benefit, not energy savings.

commonErrors.answer: Installation costs more than a conventional roof.
commonErrors.why: A drawback that does not show lower energy use.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
choices: Sedum is the only plant that can survive on a rooftop, so designers use it on every green roof.
Green roofs are the best way to prevent flooding in cities.
Older buildings cannot support green roofs, so they are impractical.
Green roofs bring several benefits to buildings and cities, though they have costs and limits.
items.answer: Green roofs bring several benefits to buildings and cities, though they have costs and limits.
items.explanation: The passage covers benefits in paragraphs 3 and 4 and drawbacks in paragraph 5.

commonErrors.answer: Green roofs are the best way to prevent flooding in cities.
commonErrors.why: Over-generalizes one benefit into the main point.

commonErrors.answer: Sedum is the only plant that can survive on a rooftop, so designers use it on every green roof.
commonErrors.why: Misreads “often choose” as “only.”

commonErrors.answer: Older buildings cannot support green roofs, so they are impractical.
commonErrors.why: Takes one drawback and treats it as the whole message.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: According to the fourth paragraph, how are dark roofs connected to the temperature of city centers?
choices: They are heavier than green roofs, so the buildings under them need much more energy for cooling.
They absorb sunlight and warm the nearby air, helping make city centers hotter.
They trap rainwater that evaporates and heats the air.
They reflect sunlight and cool the streets below them.
items.answer: They absorb sunlight and warm the nearby air, helping make city centers hotter.
items.explanation: The paragraph says dark roofs absorb sunlight and warm the air, “one reason” city centers run hotter.

commonErrors.answer: They trap rainwater that evaporates and heats the air.
commonErrors.why: Mixes up the rain discussion with the heat discussion.

commonErrors.answer: They reflect sunlight and cool the streets below them.
commonErrors.why: Reverses what dark surfaces do.

commonErrors.answer: They are heavier than green roofs, so the buildings under them need much more energy for cooling.
commonErrors.why: Weight is discussed only for wet soil.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: The last paragraph calls a green roof “part sponge, part blanket, and part garden.” What is the effect of these comparisons?
choices: They sum up the roof’s jobs of soaking up water, insulating, and growing plants.
They introduce three new benefits not discussed earlier.
They show the author doubts that green roofs will last long enough to repay their cost.
They suggest green roofs are soft and easy to damage.
items.answer: They sum up the roof’s jobs of soaking up water, insulating, and growing plants.
items.explanation: The sponge refers to rainwater, the blanket to insulation, and the garden to the plants, bringing earlier ideas together.

commonErrors.answer: They suggest green roofs are soft and easy to damage.
commonErrors.why: Reads the images as describing texture only.

commonErrors.answer: They show the author doubts that green roofs will last long enough to repay their cost.
commonErrors.why: The author is positive about the idea’s spread.

commonErrors.answer: They introduce three new benefits not discussed earlier.
commonErrors.why: Each image points back to ideas already covered.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: How does the fifth paragraph affect the development of the passage?
choices: It balances the earlier benefits by presenting drawbacks and a response to them.
It introduces another benefit related to temperature.
It reverses the central claim by arguing that green roofs are impractical for cities.
It repeats the details about plants from the second paragraph.
items.answer: It balances the earlier benefits by presenting drawbacks and a response to them.
items.explanation: Paragraph 5 begins with “not without drawbacks” and includes supporters’ replies, giving a fuller picture.

commonErrors.answer: It reverses the central claim by arguing that green roofs are impractical for cities.
commonErrors.why: The passage keeps a positive overall view.

commonErrors.answer: It introduces another benefit related to temperature.
commonErrors.why: Temperature was covered in the previous paragraph.

commonErrors.answer: It repeats the details about plants from the second paragraph.
commonErrors.why: The paragraph covers weight and cost.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: Which evidence from the passage best supports the claim that many students need a quiet place to study?
choices: The library doors close at 3:15 every afternoon.
The library has a beautiful blue carpet that was installed three years ago by the school.
The author’s cousin attends a school in another state.
In a student council survey, 140 of 200 eighth graders said they struggle to find one.
items.answer: In a student council survey, 140 of 200 eighth graders said they struggle to find one.
items.explanation: The survey results in paragraph 2 directly show that many eighth graders lack quiet study space.

commonErrors.answer: The library doors close at 3:15 every afternoon.
commonErrors.why: True, but it states when the library closes, not who needs it.

commonErrors.answer: The library has a beautiful blue carpet that was installed three years ago by the school.
commonErrors.why: A detail about decoration, not about studying.

commonErrors.answer: The author’s cousin attends a school in another state.
commonErrors.why: Offers a personal connection, not evidence about students here.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: How does the first paragraph contribute to the development of the argument?
choices: It states the author’s claim and previews the reasons developed in the paragraphs that follow.
It summarizes the survey data collected by the student council.
It tells a story about a student who could not finish homework.
It presents the strongest counterargument against the plan and then answers it with new evidence.
items.answer: It states the author’s claim and previews the reasons developed in the paragraphs that follow.
items.explanation: The paragraph states that the library should stay open and names two reasons, which paragraphs 2 and 3 then support.

commonErrors.answer: It presents the strongest counterargument against the plan and then answers it with new evidence.
commonErrors.why: The counterargument appears in the fourth paragraph.

commonErrors.answer: It summarizes the survey data collected by the student council.
commonErrors.why: The data appear in the second paragraph.

commonErrors.answer: It tells a story about a student who could not finish homework.
commonErrors.why: No such story appears in the paragraph.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: How does the author handle the argument that staying open would cost too much?
choices: The author admits the concern is reasonable and then offers a plan that limits the cost.
The author agrees that the concern is correct and then drops the proposal from the argument entirely.
The author ignores the concern and repeats the main claim.
The author claims the concern was invented by the school board.
items.answer: The author admits the concern is reasonable and then offers a plan that limits the cost.
items.explanation: The author calls the concern “fair” and then points to parent volunteers and teacher assignments.

commonErrors.answer: The author ignores the concern and repeats the main claim.
commonErrors.why: The fourth paragraph addresses the concern directly.

commonErrors.answer: The author agrees that the concern is correct and then drops the proposal from the argument entirely.
commonErrors.why: The proposal continues in the conclusion.

commonErrors.answer: The author claims the concern was invented by the school board.
commonErrors.why: Nothing in the text says this.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: Which piece of evidence is LEAST relevant to the author’s claim that the library should stay open after school?
choices: A survey found that many students struggle to find a quiet place to study.
The library’s blue carpet was installed three years ago, and blue is the author’s favorite color.
A librarian reported that more teenagers borrowed books after another library extended its hours.
Parent volunteers have offered to supervise two afternoons a week.
items.answer: The library’s blue carpet was installed three years ago, and blue is the author’s favorite color.
items.explanation: The carpet’s color and the author’s taste do not show whether students need the extra hour.

commonErrors.answer: A librarian reported that more teenagers borrowed books after another library extended its hours.
commonErrors.why: Relevant: it connects longer hours to more reading.

commonErrors.answer: A survey found that many students struggle to find a quiet place to study.
commonErrors.why: Relevant: it shows a need the library could meet.

commonErrors.answer: Parent volunteers have offered to supervise two afternoons a week.
commonErrors.why: Relevant: it addresses how the plan could be staffed.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: The author uses the example of a cousin’s school to claim, “Clearly, closing a library hurts students’ grades.” Why is this evidence weak?
choices: Evidence from another state can never apply to a school here.
The cousin’s grades are unrelated to the school’s library.
The author does not say how old the cousin is or what grade she is currently in at school.
One case does not prove that the closed library caused the grades to fall.
items.answer: One case does not prove that the closed library caused the grades to fall.
items.explanation: A single story cannot rule out other causes for lower grades, so it is insufficient to support the claim.

commonErrors.answer: Evidence from another state can never apply to a school here.
commonErrors.why: Over-generalizes; outside evidence can help if there is enough of it.

commonErrors.answer: The cousin’s grades are unrelated to the school’s library.
commonErrors.why: Overstates; the flaw is lack of proof of cause, not that no link is possible.

commonErrors.answer: The author does not say how old the cousin is or what grade she is currently in at school.
commonErrors.why: Age is not the weakness here.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: Read the sentence: “The hikers were so parched after the long climb that they drank the entire jug of water in minutes.” What does “parched” most likely mean?
choices: cold and wet
eager and cheerful
very dry and thirsty
tired and sore
items.answer: very dry and thirsty
items.explanation: Drinking the whole jug quickly suggests the hikers were very thirsty.

commonErrors.answer: tired and sore
commonErrors.why: Chooses a feeling that follows a climb but ignores the clue about drinking water.

commonErrors.answer: cold and wet
commonErrors.why: Opposite of what the clue about thirst suggests.

commonErrors.answer: eager and cheerful
commonErrors.why: Does not explain why they drank so fast.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: The word “benevolent” comes from the Latin roots bene- (“good”) and vol- (“wish”). In the sentence “The scientist’s work was benevolent; every study she led aimed to improve the village’s health,” what does “benevolent” mean?
choices: wishing to do good for others
unwilling to share knowledge
careful about spending money
wishing to be admired by others
items.answer: wishing to do good for others
items.explanation: Bene- means good and vol- means wish, and the sentence says her studies aimed to improve health.

commonErrors.answer: wishing to be admired by others
commonErrors.why: Mixes up the root meaning with fame.

commonErrors.answer: unwilling to share knowledge
commonErrors.why: Ignores the positive root bene-.

commonErrors.answer: careful about spending money
commonErrors.why: Associates “benefit” with money rather than kindness.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: The prefix dis- often means “apart” or “not.” In the sentence “The council voted to disband the committee after it finished its work,” what does “disband” mean?
choices: to praise a group publicly
to break apart a group
to rename a group
to enlarge a group
items.answer: to break apart a group
items.explanation: Dis- means apart, and the committee finished, so it was ended.

commonErrors.answer: to praise a group publicly
commonErrors.why: Ignores the meaning of dis-.

commonErrors.answer: to enlarge a group
commonErrors.why: Reverses the direction of the prefix.

commonErrors.answer: to rename a group
commonErrors.why: Fits “council voted” but not the prefix.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: Read the sentence: “The old bridge could not bear the weight of the heavy trucks.” Which meaning of “bear” is used here?
choices: to carry on a journey
to give birth to
to hold up
to put up with
items.answer: to hold up
items.explanation: A bridge supports weight, so “bear” means to hold up.

commonErrors.answer: to put up with
commonErrors.why: Chooses the common meaning “tolerate,” which does not fit a bridge.

commonErrors.answer: to give birth to
commonErrors.why: Picks the animal or family meaning rather than the one fitting the context.

commonErrors.answer: to carry on a journey
commonErrors.why: Interprets “carry” as moving something rather than supporting it.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: Read the sentence: “Although the committee seemed ready to quarrel, the mayor’s calm words had a mollifying effect, and the shouting soon died away.” What does “mollifying” most likely mean?
choices: provoking
soothing
distracting
confusing
items.answer: soothing
items.explanation: The “calm words” and the dying shouting show that the effect was soothing.

commonErrors.answer: provoking
commonErrors.why: Reverses the meaning; the shouting stopped, not grew.

commonErrors.answer: confusing
commonErrors.why: The sentence says the shouting ended, not that people were puzzled.

commonErrors.answer: distracting
commonErrors.why: Suggests turning attention away rather than calming anger.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: The Latin root aud- means “to hear.” In the sentence “The announcement was barely audible over the roar of the crowd,” what does “audible” mean?
choices: easy to understand
pleasant to listen to
able to be heard
worth repeating aloud
items.answer: able to be heard
items.explanation: Aud- means hear, and the crowd noise made the announcement hard to hear.

commonErrors.answer: easy to understand
commonErrors.why: Confuses hearing with understanding.

commonErrors.answer: pleasant to listen to
commonErrors.why: Adds a quality of enjoyment that the root does not carry.

commonErrors.answer: worth repeating aloud
commonErrors.why: Reads aud- as “speak” instead of “hear.”

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: Read the sentence: “The ambassador’s reply was deliberately ambiguous; both sides left the room convinced she had agreed with them.” What does “ambiguous” most likely mean?
choices: lengthy and detailed
open to more than one meaning
dishonest and false
forceful and direct
items.answer: open to more than one meaning
items.explanation: Both sides thought she agreed with them, so her reply could be understood in two ways.

commonErrors.answer: forceful and direct
commonErrors.why: Reverses the clue that each side heard its own meaning.

commonErrors.answer: dishonest and false
commonErrors.why: Confuses vagueness with lying.

commonErrors.answer: lengthy and detailed
commonErrors.why: Does not match the idea of unclear meaning.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: Read the sentence: “The idea was so novel that no one at the meeting had heard anything like it.” What does “novel” mean here?
choices: long and fictional
new and original
familiar and ordinary
confusing and unclear
items.answer: new and original
items.explanation: The clue “no one had heard anything like it” shows the idea was new.

commonErrors.answer: long and fictional
commonErrors.why: Uses the noun meaning, a book, instead of the adjective.

commonErrors.answer: familiar and ordinary
commonErrors.why: Reverses the clue “no one had heard anything like it.”

commonErrors.answer: confusing and unclear
commonErrors.why: Assumes new ideas must be hard to follow.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: Read the sentence: “Her voice was a warm blanket on a cold night.” What does this metaphor suggest about her voice?
choices: It was loud and heavy.
It was quiet and hard to hear.
It was gentle but not sincere.
It was comforting and soothing.
items.answer: It was comforting and soothing.
items.explanation: A warm blanket on a cold night brings comfort, so her voice does too.

commonErrors.answer: It was loud and heavy.
commonErrors.why: Applies the blanket’s weight instead of its comfort.

commonErrors.answer: It was gentle but not sincere.
commonErrors.why: Adds an idea about honesty that the image does not suggest.

commonErrors.answer: It was quiet and hard to hear.
commonErrors.why: Mixes up warmth with softness of volume.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: Read the sentence: “The twins let the cat out of the bag about the surprise party.” What does the idiom mean?
choices: They ruined the party decorations.
They forgot the date of the party.
They revealed a secret.
They adopted a new pet.
items.answer: They revealed a secret.
items.explanation: “Let the cat out of the bag” means to reveal a secret, and the party was a surprise.

commonErrors.answer: They ruined the party decorations.
commonErrors.why: Takes the idiom literally as spoiling something physical.

commonErrors.answer: They adopted a new pet.
commonErrors.why: Reads the animal literally.

commonErrors.answer: They forgot the date of the party.
commonErrors.why: Confuses revealing with forgetting.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: Read the sentence: “The marathon runner finished all twenty-six miles without a scratch, then twisted her ankle stepping off the curb outside the finish line.” Why is this situation ironic?
choices: She expected to win but finished in last place.
She survived the hardest part safely but was hurt by an ordinary step.
She was injured before the race and ran anyway.
She was hurt on a curb, and curbs are always dangerous.
items.answer: She survived the hardest part safely but was hurt by an ordinary step.
items.explanation: Irony arises because the outcome is the opposite of what we expect: a small step causes the injury after the long race.

commonErrors.answer: She expected to win but finished in last place.
commonErrors.why: Invents an expectation that is not in the sentence.

commonErrors.answer: She was injured before the race and ran anyway.
commonErrors.why: Reverses the order of events.

commonErrors.answer: She was hurt on a curb, and curbs are always dangerous.
commonErrors.why: States a general claim instead of the contrast in the event.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: Chapter is to book as scene is to ___. Which word best completes this analogy?
choices: play
curtain
audience
actor
items.answer: play
items.explanation: A chapter is a part of a book, and a scene is a part of a play.

commonErrors.answer: actor
commonErrors.why: Pairs a part with a performer, not a part with its whole.

commonErrors.answer: audience
commonErrors.why: Pairs a part with the people who watch it.

commonErrors.answer: curtain
commonErrors.why: Pairs a part with an object on the stage, not the whole.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: Read the sentence: “The company announced that it was ‘letting go’ of a quarter of its staff.” What effect does the phrase “letting go” have?
choices: It shows that the workers chose to leave on their own.
It softens the harsh idea of firing workers.
It makes the layoffs sound more severe than they are.
It shows that the workers were promoted.
items.answer: It softens the harsh idea of firing workers.
items.explanation: A euphemism replaces a blunt phrase such as “firing” with a gentler one.

commonErrors.answer: It shows that the workers chose to leave on their own.
commonErrors.why: Reads “let go” as the workers’ choice.

commonErrors.answer: It makes the layoffs sound more severe than they are.
commonErrors.why: Reverses the effect, which is to make the news gentler.

commonErrors.answer: It shows that the workers were promoted.
commonErrors.why: Confuses a positive-sounding phrase with a promotion.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: A shopper who avoids spending money could be described as thrifty, frugal, economical, or stingy. Which word has the most negative connotation?
choices: thrifty
economical
stingy
frugal
items.answer: stingy
items.explanation: “Stingy” suggests selfishness, while the other words suggest wise care with money.

commonErrors.answer: thrifty
commonErrors.why: Treats a positive word as a negative one.

commonErrors.answer: frugal
commonErrors.why: Treats a neutral-to-positive word as negative.

commonErrors.answer: economical
commonErrors.why: Ignores that this word suggests wise use of money.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: Read the sentence: “The negotiation was a tightrope walk; one careless remark could send the whole deal crashing down.” What does the figurative phrase mean?
choices: The talks were taking place at a great height.
The deal had already failed before the talks began.
The talks demanded great care to avoid a ruinous mistake.
The negotiators were skilled circus performers.
items.answer: The talks demanded great care to avoid a ruinous mistake.
items.explanation: A tightrope walk requires balance, so the phrase shows that one error could ruin the talks.

commonErrors.answer: The negotiators were skilled circus performers.
commonErrors.why: Takes the image literally.

commonErrors.answer: The talks were taking place at a great height.
commonErrors.why: Reads the image as describing a location.

commonErrors.answer: The deal had already failed before the talks began.
commonErrors.why: Ignores that the sentence says the deal “could” fall.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: “To ___ the poem, the class examined each stanza and discussed how its parts fit together.”
choices: memorize
abbreviate
applaud
analyze
items.answer: analyze
items.explanation: Examining parts and how they fit together is what it means to analyze.

commonErrors.answer: memorize
commonErrors.why: Confuses studying parts with learning by heart.

commonErrors.answer: applaud
commonErrors.why: Mistakes discussing a poem for praising it.

commonErrors.answer: abbreviate
commonErrors.why: Mixes up examining with shortening.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: “The coach repeated the final instruction twice to ___ how important it was.”
choices: estimate
emphasize
conceal
excuse
items.answer: emphasize
items.explanation: Repeating an instruction stresses its importance, which is what “emphasize” means.

commonErrors.answer: conceal
commonErrors.why: Reverses the purpose of repeating something.

commonErrors.answer: excuse
commonErrors.why: Confuses stressing with forgiving.

commonErrors.answer: estimate
commonErrors.why: Confuses stressing with guessing a number.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: “Only evidence that is ___ to the claim belongs in an argument; unrelated facts weaken it.”
choices: sufficient
familiar
identical
relevant
items.answer: relevant
items.explanation: The sentence calls for evidence that is connected to the claim, which is what relevant means.

commonErrors.answer: identical
commonErrors.why: Mistakes connected for exactly the same.

commonErrors.answer: familiar
commonErrors.why: Mistakes well known for related.

commonErrors.answer: sufficient
commonErrors.why: Confuses having enough evidence with having related evidence.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: Which sentence uses the word “contrast” correctly?
choices: The two twins looked so contrasting that no one could tell them apart.
The contrast of the two trains arrived at noon.
The author draws a contrast between the quiet village and the busy city.
She contrasted the cake by mixing the sugar and the flour.
items.answer: The author draws a contrast between the quiet village and the busy city.
items.explanation: A contrast points out differences, and a quiet village and a busy city differ.

commonErrors.answer: The two twins looked so contrasting that no one could tell them apart.
commonErrors.why: Uses “contrasting” as if it meant “alike.”

commonErrors.answer: She contrasted the cake by mixing the sugar and the flour.
commonErrors.why: Uses the verb as if it meant “make” or “prepare.”

commonErrors.answer: The contrast of the two trains arrived at noon.
commonErrors.why: Uses the noun as if it were a plural subject.

items.subject: ela
items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: “The second witness’s story helped to ___ the first account, since every detail matched.”
choices: summarize
postpone
refute
corroborate
items.answer: corroborate
items.explanation: Matching details confirm the first account, and corroborate means to confirm.

commonErrors.answer: refute
commonErrors.why: Reverses the meaning; matching details support rather than disprove.

commonErrors.answer: summarize
commonErrors.why: Confuses confirming with shortening.

commonErrors.answer: postpone
commonErrors.why: Confuses confirming with delaying.
